stem: During living donor informed consent, which donor right must the coordinator confirm per standard references?

options.text: The donor may decline to donate at any time
The donor must proceed once evaluation begins and cannot withdraw
Only the recipient surgeon may decide whether donation proceeds
Withdrawal after consent is prohibited by federal law

explanation.rationale_correct: Living donor informed consent requires confirmation that the donor is free from inducement and coercion and has been informed that he or she can decline to donate at any time.

rationale_incorrect.B: Donors may decline at any time rather than being locked in once evaluation begins.
rationale_incorrect.C: Donor autonomy includes the right to withdraw; separate live donor team advocacy supports donor interests.
rationale_incorrect.D: Federal law prohibits organ sales; it does not prohibit donors from declining donation.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Care of Living Donors → F. Elements Included in Education and Informed Consent → 1.c.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Has been informed that he or she can decline to donate at any time

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 7 → F. Elements Included in Education and Informed Consent → 1.a.–c. (donor may decline at any time; free from coercion); PDF p. 340 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Living-donor withdrawal-right angle distinct from separate live donor team (cctc-1045) and follow-up commitment (cctc-1030); anchor verified on Cupples p. 340.

stem: A coordinator is updating BK virus teaching for kidney transplant recipients. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: BK virus reactivation after kidney transplantation is common, with prevalence around 45% to 50%.
Every episode of BK reactivation inevitably progresses to graft loss.
BK reactivation may cause tubulointerstitial nephritis.
BK virus transmission in the general population occurs primarily through the respiratory route.

explanation.rationale_correct: BK reactivation is common in kidney recipients but progresses to nephropathy only occasionally; it may cause tubulointerstitial nephritis, and population transmission is primarily respiratory. Statement II is false because not all reactivation leads to graft loss.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement II is false; statement III is also correct.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement I is also true; statement II is false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement II is false—not all BK reactivation progresses to graft loss.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → J. Polyomaviruses → 2. BK virus → b.–c.i.

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).

stem: When educating a lung transplant recipient about cytomegalovirus (CMV) long-term allograft effects, which complication should the coordinator include?

explanation.rationale_correct: Organ-specific CMV effects on allografts include bronchiolitis obliterans in lung transplant recipients.

rationale_incorrect.B: Vanishing bile duct syndrome is the listed CMV organ-specific effect for liver allografts.
rationale_incorrect.C: Coronary artery vasculopathy is the listed CMV organ-specific effect for heart allografts.
rationale_incorrect.D: Oral aversion is an intestinal transplant feeding complication unrelated to CMV lung effects.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → CMV → 8. Organ-specific effects on allograft → c.

stem: When scheduling pretransplant immunizations for an adult or pediatric candidate, how long should live vaccines be separated from the transplant procedure per standard references?

options.text: At least 4 weeks between live vaccine administration and transplant
Live vaccines may be given the day before surgery without restriction
Live vaccines are required immediately after transplant in all candidates
No interval is needed between live vaccines and transplantation

explanation.rationale_correct: Candidates should wait at least 4 weeks between administration of live vaccines and the transplant procedure for all adult and pediatric candidates.

rationale_incorrect.B: Live vaccines require a minimum 4-week interval before transplant rather than same-day administration.
rationale_incorrect.C: Live vaccines are generally avoided after transplantation; pretransplant timing follows the 4-week rule.
rationale_incorrect.D: A defined waiting period is required between live vaccines and transplant.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Recommended Pretransplant Immunizations → e.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Wait at least 4 weeks between administration of live vaccines and transplant procedure for all adult and pediatric candidates
